title: US Inflation Is About to Hit a Three-Year High. Every Indian Immigrant Should Pay Attention.
excerpt: May's consumer price index is expected to show the sharpest annual increase since April 2023, driven by soaring energy costs from the Middle East war. Real wages are falling, and the Fed is unlikely to offer relief.
body:
The US Labor Department will release May's Consumer Price Index on Wednesday, and economists are bracing for an ugly number. The consensus forecast, compiled by Reuters, expects the CPI to have risen 4.2 per cent year-on-year — the largest annual increase since April 2023 and the third straight month of accelerating inflation. On a monthly basis, prices are expected to have jumped 0.5 per cent after a 0.6 per cent gain in April.

For the roughly 4.4 million Indian-born residents of the United States — including H-1B workers, green card holders, naturalised citizens, and their families — this is not an abstract economic indicator. It is the gas bill, the rent cheque, the grocery run, and the mortgage payment. And it is about to get harder.

## The War Premium

The primary driver is energy. The national average gasoline price surged 8.8 per cent in May to $4.60 a gallon, according to the US Energy Information Administration. At one point, pump prices had spiked more than 50 per cent since the US and Israel attacked Iran at the end of February, triggering the prolonged blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

"The top-line increase in inflation will outpace wage growth for the second consecutive month," said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM. "What that means is Americans are seeing their paycheck decline in real terms, which, if it were sustained, would tend to suggest we're going to have a challenge around household consumption in the second half of the year."

Real wages declining for two months running is a critical threshold. It means that even as nominal paychecks grow, the cost of living is growing faster — a squeeze that hits disproportionately hard in the high-cost metropolitan areas where Indian immigrants are concentrated: the Bay Area, Seattle, New York, New Jersey, the Dallas-Fort Worth corridor, and the Washington, D.C. suburbs.

## What the Fed Will (and Won't) Do

The Federal Reserve tracks a different inflation measure — the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index — for its 2 per cent target. But all inflation gauges are now running well above that mark. Financial markets have begun pricing in the possibility of a rate hike, a dramatic reversal from the rate cuts investors expected just six months ago.

Economists remain divided. Some, like James Knightley, chief international economist at ING, say a rate hike would only be triggered if core inflation — which strips out food and energy — shows signs of energy costs bleeding into other categories. Core CPI is expected at 2.9 per cent year-on-year, up from 2.8 per cent in April. A 0.3 per cent monthly gain would be manageable. But if the number surprises to the upside, the calculus changes fast.

Others see a silver lining. Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander US Capital Markets, believes May could mark the peak for headline inflation, noting that gasoline prices have retreated somewhat in recent weeks amid the fragile ceasefire. Tariff pass-through, which added roughly 63 to 70 basis points to prices earlier this year, also appears to be decelerating.

## The NRI Squeeze

For Indian immigrants, the inflation picture creates pressure on multiple fronts simultaneously.

**Mortgage and housing costs.** With the Fed holding rates at elevated levels — and the 10-year Treasury yield pushing higher on inflation fears — mortgage rates remain stubbornly above 7 per cent. Indian-American families in tech hubs who purchased homes during the post-pandemic surge are locked into high payments, while prospective buyers face an increasingly hostile market.

**H-1B and job market risks.** Tighter economic conditions can shift immigration sentiment. Tech layoffs earlier this year already rattled the H-1B workforce. If inflation forces the Fed to tighten further, the resulting slowdown could reduce the hiring that justifies visa sponsorship.

**Remittance purchasing power.** The rupee has been under sustained pressure in 2026, weakened by India's own trade deficit and foreign fund outflows. But the strength of the dollar in a high-rate environment has partially offset that for NRI remitters. If the Fed pivots hawkish, the dollar could strengthen further — a mixed blessing that helps remittance senders but hurts India's import bill.

**Portfolio impact.** Friday's sharp selloff in US markets — with the Nasdaq dropping over 4 per cent on AI valuation concerns — wiped roughly $2.5 trillion in market value. Indian-American investors with heavy exposure to tech through 401(k) plans and individual brokerage accounts felt the pain directly. Inflation running hot makes a recovery harder by keeping the rate environment restrictive.

## The Bigger Picture

The inflation report arrives against a backdrop of renewed military escalation. On Tuesday evening, the US launched strikes against Iranian air defence and radar sites near the Strait of Hormuz — a "proportional response" to Monday's downing of a US Apache helicopter. Oil prices climbed about 1 per cent in early Asian trade, and any sustained energy price spike would feed directly back into the next month's CPI.

For Indian immigrants navigating the American cost-of-living crisis, the calculus is straightforward: plan for inflation to stay elevated through the summer, diversify savings out of cash and into inflation-hedged instruments, and don't count on rate relief from the Fed anytime soon. The war that raised these prices is not over. The drought that could raise food prices has barely begun.
